steps.body: Now flip the match: same TOPS, different bottoms. 2/3 vs 2/8 — two pieces each, but two of WHICH pieces? Thirds are slabs; eighths are slivers. The same count of bigger pieces is more: **2/3 wins**. The bottom dial from chapter 1 is back.

widget.prompt: One piece of the bar is shown. Slide the cut count to make that single piece as BIG as it can be.
widget.lowFeedback: You've hit the slider's coarsest cut — no bigger pieces available here.
widget.highFeedback: Finer cuts shrink your piece — slide the other way for bigger slabs.
widget.successFeedback: A 2-cut makes the biggest pieces on this slider — which is exactly why 1/2 beats 1/6 beats 1/8. Fewer cuts, bigger pieces.

predict.prompt: You'll slide the CUT COUNT on one bar. Predict: to make a single piece as big as possible, the cut count should be…
predict.reveal: Fewer cuts, bigger pieces — the bottom number counts CUTS, not size. Watch the piece shrink as the denominator grows: that's the big-number reflex, disarmed.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents compare same num.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for compare same num must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines compare same num.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Two slabs from a 3-cut beat two slivers from an 8-cut — same count, much bigger pieces.
The bottoms set piece size: thirds are big, eighths are small, and the counts match at 2 each.

widget.prompt: Which is more of the same pan of brownies: 2/3 or 2/8?
widget.rightFeedback: The big-number reflex! The 8 means an 8-way cut — smaller pieces, not more brownie. Two slivers lose to two slabs.
widget.equalFeedback: Only the COUNTS match. The piece sizes don't — a third of the pan dwarfs an eighth of it.
widget.successFeedback: Two big third-slabs against two little eighth-slivers — the slabs win easily.

steps.body: The fix, said plainly: **on the bottom, a bigger number means more cuts, which means smaller pieces.** Whole-number instinct runs backwards downstairs. So when the tops match, the fraction with the SMALLER bottom holds the bigger pieces — and wins.

explanationVariants: The 10 doesn't add brownie — it adds CUTS. Ten-way pieces are slivers; three of them lose to three quarter-slabs.
Test with the bar: shade 3 of 10 pieces, then 3 of 4 — the 3/4 shading visibly swallows the other.

widget.prompt: Priya says 3/10 is bigger than 3/4 'because 10 is bigger than 4.' What should we tell Priya?

options.label: Ten cuts make smaller pieces, so 3/10 is less than 3/4.
options.feedback: The bottom counts cuts, not size. More cuts, smaller pieces — so the bigger bottom LOSES when tops match.

options.label: Ten cuts make larger pieces, so 3/10 is greater than 3/4.
options.feedback: Picture both: a bar cut in 10 vs the same bar cut in 4. Which single piece would you grab? The quarter — and she took three of each.

options.label: Add the top and bottom numbers to compare 3/10 and 3/4.
options.feedback: Adding 3+10 and 3+4 mixes the numbers' jobs. The fix is knowing what the bottom MEANS: cut count, so bigger = smaller pieces.

options.label: Tenths are not real fractions, so they cannot be compared.
options.feedback: Tenths are perfectly real — just small. That smallness is exactly the point of the fix.

steps.body: Match each duel to its winner.

widget.prompt: Same tops in every duel — connect each to its winner and the reason.

right.label: 1/3 — a third is the bigger single piece

pairErrors.feedback: That answer belongs to the 3/4 duel. In 1/3 vs 1/8, the smaller bottom (3) makes the bigger piece — 1/3 wins its own fight.

widget.missFeedback: Tops match in every duel — so the SMALLER bottom (fewer cuts, bigger pieces) wins each one.
widget.successFeedback: Three duels, one rule: matching counts of bigger pieces win — the smaller bottom takes every fight.

explanationVariants: All tops are 4, so piece size decides: fifths beat sevenths beat ninths — 4/5 > 4/7 > 4/9.
Fewer cuts, bigger pieces, bigger amount — the bottoms rank in reverse.

options.feedback: Same count (4), so the coarsest cut wins: fifths, then sevenths, then ninths.
That's the big-number reflex ranking. On the bottom, bigger means MORE cuts and smaller pieces — the order runs the other way.

options.label: All equal — the tops match
options.feedback: Matching tops only match the COUNT. Four fifth-slabs hold far more than four ninth-slivers.

options.label: 4/7 is biggest
options.feedback: Sevenths sit in the middle — fifths are the coarsest cut here, so 4/5 leads.

hints: The pizzas are the same size — only the CUTS differ.
Jo's slices come from a 3-cut; Kai's from an 8-cut. Whose slices are bigger?
Same slice count, different slice sizes.
explanationVariants: Both took 2 slices, but Jo's are third-size slabs and Kai's are eighth-size slivers — same count of bigger pieces means Jo has more: 2/3 > 2/8.
Check with a trade: Kai would need his 2 eighths grown more than two-and-a-half times to match Jo's 2 thirds.

widget.prompt: Two same-size pizzas. Jo takes 2 slices of the one cut into 3; Kai takes 2 slices of the one cut into 8. Who has more pizza? (Jo's bar is first, Kai's second.)
widget.rightFeedback: The reflex, one last time: the 8 cut his pizza into MORE, SMALLER slices. His two slivers lose to Jo's two slabs.
widget.equalFeedback: The counts match; the slices don't. A slice's size comes from the cut, and Jo's cut was coarser.
widget.successFeedback: Two slabs beat two slivers: 2/3 > 2/8, because the 3-cut makes the bigger pieces.

takeaways: Same tops = same count, so PIECE SIZE decides — the smaller bottom wins.
On the bottom, bigger means more cuts and smaller pieces — instinct runs backwards there.
Counting pieces only works when the pieces match (rule one's fine print).

concept.body: Quick rewind. Would you rather split a candy bar with **2 friends or with 7**? Fewer sharers, bigger shares. The bottom counts the sharers — so when the tops match, the SMALLER bottom hands out the bigger pieces.

explanationVariants: A 4-cut makes bigger pieces than a 6-cut — one of each, and the fourth wins.
Fewer sharers (4 vs 6) means a bigger share for each.

widget.prompt: Which is more of the same bar: 1/4 or 1/6?

options.feedback: Four-way pieces are bigger than six-way pieces — 1/4 wins.
The 6 means MORE cuts — smaller pieces. One sixth is the smaller share.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: Same count (one piece each), different sizes — the 4-cut piece is half again as big.
